lyocell.types: Standard lyocell fibrillates when wet-abraded, and finishers either suppress this or exploit it for a peach-skin surface. Cross-linked low-fibrillation grades are treated during fiber production so that fabrics stay smooth through garment dyeing and home laundering, suiting knitwear and bright colors. Staple lyocell is made in several finenesses and cut lengths for cotton-type or wool-type spinning, including micro grades for very soft, dense fabrics, and some producers offer filament lyocell with a silk-like luster. Dope-dyed lyocell is colored before spinning. Lenzing sells lyocell under its TENCEL brand and, under the REFIBRA name, lyocell made partly from pulp that includes cotton scraps. Other producers make generic lyocell, so the brand tag, not the fiber name, identifies Lenzing fiber.
lyocell.fabrics: Lyocell is widely used in denim, alone or blended with cotton, where it adds drape, a cool touch and a soft, sometimes sueded surface after enzyme or stone washing. It is woven into shirting, chambray and twill trousers, and into sateen and percale sheets marketed for cool sleep. Jersey and interlock knits appear in T-shirts, dresses and underwear, and fibrillated finishes give sand-washed blouses. It is blended with wool, silk or linen for drape and with cotton through siro spinning, where two strands are spun together, for smooth yarns. Nonwoven lyocell is used in wipes and technical products.
lyocell.quality: Check for fibrillation on dark colors: a pale, frosted haze, especially along seams and folds, shows the finish was not controlled and will worsen with wear. A deliberate peach-skin fabric should look uniform. Smooth lyocell should feel cool, heavy and fluid rather than papery. Look at the generic name on the content line, since TENCEL can mean lyocell or modal, and treat pulp, recycling or solvent recovery statements as producer claims tied to specific fibers. For sheets, weave and yarn matter more than thread count, which is less meaningful for lyocell's smooth filaments and fine staple. Wrinkle recovery is better than viscose, but pure lyocell shirting still creases.
pros: It keeps most of its strength when wet, so it is more stable in washing than regular viscose.
It feels smooth and cool with a fluid drape and good moisture uptake.
Its solvent is recovered at a very high rate in a closed process, according to producers.
It blends well with cotton, wool and silk and suits both woven and knitted fabrics.
cons: Wet abrasion can fibrillate the surface, leaving a frosted, hairy look on dark colors.
Fabrics can stiffen after line drying and may need tumbling or steaming to soften.
It usually costs more than viscose and cotton of similar weight.
Brand names can obscure whether a product is lyocell, modal or a small-percentage blend.
lyocell.impact: Lyocell avoids carbon disulfide, and its NMMO solvent is recovered in a closed loop, so the main footprint questions are pulp sourcing and the energy used to evaporate and recover the solvent. In a 2010 life cycle assessment of Lenzing fibers published in Resources, Conservation and Recycling, Shen, Worrell and Patel ranked Tencel lyocell among the lowest overall impacts of the fibers studied, which also included viscose, modal, cotton, PET and polypropylene; results were specific to the plants, energy mixes and pulp supply of that producer. Canopy's Hot Button Report also covers lyocell producers' forest-sourcing risk. Lyocell made partly from cotton scraps reduces virgin pulp demand, but recycled content shares are producer claims.
lyocell.care: Wash lyocell at 30 C, or up to 40 C if the label allows, on a gentle cycle, inside out and in an uncrowded drum to limit the abrasion that causes fibrillation. Use a mild detergent without chlorine bleach. Tumble dry on low and remove promptly, or line dry and then soften briefly in the dryer or with steam, since line-dried lyocell can feel stiff. Iron at medium heat, about 150 C (two dots), preferably with steam or on the reverse for dark colors. Store as you would cotton. Once a frosted haze appears it cannot be reversed at home, so gentle washing from the start matters.
faq: Is TENCEL the same as lyocell?

Not exactly. TENCEL is Lenzing's brand name, used for both its lyocell and its modal fibers. Lyocell is the generic fiber name for cellulose spun from a direct organic solvent. Check the content label: 'TENCEL lyocell' and 'TENCEL modal' are different fibers.
Why does my dark lyocell shirt look frosted?

That haze is fibrillation. Wet lyocell fibers can split into fine surface fibrils when rubbed during washing, and the fibrils scatter light, making dark colors look pale. Washing inside out, on gentle cycles and in smaller loads slows it, but it cannot be fully undone.

Many people find lyocell sheets smooth and cool, because the fiber absorbs moisture and drapes closely. They cost more than cotton and need gentle washing to avoid fibrillation. Comparative sleep-temperature claims come mostly from sellers and have limited independent testing.

It can have a lower footprint than viscose or conventional cotton because its solvent is recovered and it avoids carbon disulfide. Results depend on the producer's energy, pulp source and forest certification, so check producer documentation rather than relying on the generic name.
notable: A 2010 life cycle study found Lenzing's Tencel, along with its Austrian-made modal and viscose, among the lowest overall impacts of the fibers it compared.
Fibrillation, usually a flaw, is deliberately induced to create the soft peach-skin or sand-washed surface on some lyocell fabrics.
